name: Paluai
confidence_why: The only description of Paluai stress is Schokkin's reference grammar (2014 thesis, published 2020), which states that each word has one primary stress on the penult or the final syllable, largely predictable from syllable shape and word class but with many lexical exceptions, and no other source has described the language.
catalog_citation: Schokkin, Dineke. 2014. A grammar of Paluai, the language of Baluan Island, Papua New Guinea. PhD thesis, James Cook University (researchonline.jcu.edu.au/28026; PDF via the Internet Archive 20240626).
catalog_quote: In each word, there is one syllable that receives primary stress. In words that contain three or more syllables, mostly there will be one syllable with secondary stress in addition to the one with primary stress. This is never a syllable adjacent to the syllable that receives primary stress. Stress assignment is to a large extent predictable and is either penultimate or final. However, lexical stress shows tendencies rather than strict rules and for every generalisation there are many exceptions. ... Stress assignment of CV.CV and CV.VC forms is most straightforward: these are stressed on the penultimate syllable without exception, regardless of word class. ... With regard to CV.CVC disyllabic forms, the following observations can be made. tone_statements.citation: Schokkin, Gerda (2013). A grammar of Paluai, the language of Baluan Island, Papua New Guinea. James Cook University.
tone_statements.quote: Prosody refers to suprasegmental features of speech, as opposed to segmental phonology. Relevant features for Paluai include stress and intonation. 2.3.1 Stress In words that contain more than one syllable, there are some syllables that are more prominent than others. This prominence is due to more acoustic energy, mainly loudness and pitch, and can be conveniently called ‘stress’. Length is not a factor in stress assignment: Paluai does not have contrastive vowel length and stressed vowels do not appear to be longer than unstressed vowels.
tone_statements.summary: Prosody analysed as word stress plus sentence intonation only; pitch is a correlate of stress and of intonation (one main pitch rise per sentence); no lexical tone is described.

audit.reasoning: The record rests on the only full description of Paluai, Schokkin's 516-pp reference-grammar thesis (2014), which we hold and whose stress section I re-read (pp. 52-60): every fragment of the deciding quotation is verbatim at the stated pages, and the classification 'variable' (one primary stress, penultimate or final, word-class and syllable-shape tendencies with pervasive exceptions, stress-attracting -ek, two stress minimal pairs) matches the text. Glottolog's five descriptive refs are all by Schokkin; Crossref turns up no separate stress/prosody or instrumental study. The only upgrade is the paywalled 2020 De Gruyter Mouton revision (ch. 2 Phonology, pp. 8-56), same author and data, low priority. Nothing open was available to download
